mainEntity.name: How large a gap can veneers realistically close?

acceptedAnswer.text: Veneers are generally considered most suitable for small to moderate interdental gaps. There is no universally defined measurement, as suitability depends on several factors — including how the gap affects your bite and the proportions of your individual teeth. Attempting to close a very large gap with veneers alone could result in teeth that appear disproportionately wide or that adversely affect your bite. A clinical assessment will allow your dentist to advise on what is achievable and whether alternative approaches such as orthodontics might be more appropriate in your particular case.

mainEntity.name: Will veneers damage my natural teeth?

acceptedAnswer.text: Porcelain veneers typically require a small amount of enamel to be permanently removed from the tooth surface so that the veneer can be fitted without appearing bulky. This means the process is largely irreversible. Composite veneers, however, can often be placed with minimal or no enamel reduction. Your dentist will explain exactly what preparation is required and ensure you understand the implications before any treatment begins. Providing you maintain good oral hygiene and attend regular check-ups, the underlying tooth can remain healthy.

mainEntity.name: How long do dental veneers typically last?

acceptedAnswer.text: With appropriate care, porcelain veneers can last ten years or more, and in some cases considerably longer. Composite veneers tend to have a shorter lifespan and may require more regular maintenance, repair, or replacement. Longevity is influenced by factors such as oral hygiene habits, diet, whether you grind your teeth, and how well you attend routine dental appointments. Your dental team will give you realistic guidance based on your individual circumstances and the type of veneers recommended for you.

mainEntity.name: Can veneers be used instead of braces to close a gap?

acceptedAnswer.text: Veneers and orthodontic treatment work in fundamentally different ways. Orthodontics physically moves the teeth into a new position, whilst veneers change the appearance of the tooth surface without altering the underlying position. For small gaps that do not involve the bite, veneers can be a quicker cosmetic solution. However, for larger gaps or cases involving bite misalignment, orthodontic treatment may be clinically preferable. In some cases, patients may benefit from a combination of both approaches. Your dentist will help you understand which option suits your needs.

Most patients find veneer treatment to be a comfortable experience. For porcelain veneers, local anaesthetic is typically used during the tooth preparation stage to ensure you do not feel any discomfort. Composite veneers, which often require minimal preparation, are generally associated with very little if any discomfort. Some patients experience mild sensitivity in the days following preparation, but this usually settles. Your dental team will discuss what to expect at each stage of treatment and ensure you feel at ease throughout the process.

mainEntity.name: What are the alternatives to veneers for closing a front tooth gap?

acceptedAnswer.text: Several alternatives may be considered depending on the size of the gap, the condition of the surrounding teeth, and your overall dental health. These include orthodontic treatment (such as fixed braces or clear aligners), dental bonding (which uses composite resin applied directly to the teeth in a single visit with no enamel removal), or in some cases, crown treatment. Each option carries its own set of considerations, advantages, and limitations. A clinical consultation is the most reliable way to identify which approach is most appropriate for you.
